claims.claim: Le Guin's count of the hundred-syllable Tolkien sample gives 45 one-syllable words out of 72 words.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Stress-Rhythm in Poetry and Prose', The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)

claims.claim: Le Guin says her samples are far too small and her stress-counting too subjective for any conclusions to be drawn.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Stress-Rhythm in Poetry and Prose', The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: too subjective for any conclusions at all to be drawn

claims.claim: Le Guin observes that Jane Austen's stress-count nearly matching the textbook's shows stress-counting alone cannot indicate the quality of prose.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Stress-Rhythm in Poetry and Prose', The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: merely counting stresses is not going to give us any solid

claims.claim: Le Guin's counts show that in even a readable textbook more than half the words are polysyllables.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Stress-Rhythm in Poetry and Prose', The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: in even a readable textbook more than half the words

claims.claim: Le Guin's counts show Mark Twain using more one-syllable words than the folktale sample.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Stress-Rhythm in Poetry and Prose', The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: that Mark Twain uses more one-syllable words than a folktale

claims.claim: Le Guin's counts show Woolf writing the shortest sentences of the eight samples and Austen the longest.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Stress-Rhythm in Poetry and Prose', The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: Woolf writes the shortest sentences of the lot and Austen the longest

claims.claim: Le Guin asserts that the power of deliberate repetition in a narrative is both great and legitimate.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Stress-Rhythm in Poetry and Prose', The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: deliberate repetition in a narrative is both great and legitimate

claims.claim: Le Guin states flatly that rhythm is repetition.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Stress-Rhythm in Poetry and Prose', The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)

claims.claim: Le Guin says a narrative's coherence is established by inner references and backward- or forward-looking semirepetitions.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Stress-Rhythm in Poetry and Prose', The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: coherence is established by inner references and backward-looking or forward-looking
claims.page: 'Repetition of Images, Actions, Moods, and Themes'

claims.claim: Le Guin warns that if the rhythms become predictable the coherence of the story is mechanical.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Stress-Rhythm in Poetry and Prose', The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: If the rhythms become predictable, the coherence of the story
claims.page: 'Repetition of Images, Actions, Moods, and Themes'

claims.claim: Le Guin describes textbook prose as hobbling along clogged by a superfluity of unnecessary and understressed polysyllables.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (2001), in The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: clogged by a superfluity of egregiously unnecessary and understressed polysyllables
claims.page: early pages of the essay, on stress ratios

claims.claim: Le Guin gives the ratio for narrative prose as one beat in every two to four syllables, against one in two or three for poetry.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (2001), in The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: that ratio goes down to one beat in two to four
claims.page: early pages of the essay, on stress ratios

claims.claim: Le Guin says Tolkien's prose runs to the normal narrative ratio of one stress every two to four syllables.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (2001), in The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: one stress every two to four syllables
claims.page: early pages of the essay, on stress ratios

claims.claim: Le Guin describes the speech of the elves and noble folk such as Aragorn as having a dignified, often stately gait but no regular stress-beat.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (2001), in The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: a dignified, often stately gait, but not a regular stress-beat
claims.page: on metric passages in the Trilogy

claims.claim: Le Guin says Tolkien's narrative moves in balanced cadences in passages of epic action yet remains pure prose.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (2001), in The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: balanced cadences in passages of epic action
claims.page: on metric passages in the Trilogy
